cse-1999-a-1.approach: Use the fact that an average can never exceed the largest value being averaged: if $X<5$ everywhere then $E[X]<5$.

steps.title: Contrapositive
steps.body: Suppose $X(\omega)<5$ at every sample point. Then $E[X]=\sum_\omega X(\omega)P(\omega)<\sum_\omega 5\,P(\omega)=5$, contradicting $E[X]=5$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: So at least one sample point has $X\ge 5$. Equality alone or strict excess alone is not forced: $X\equiv5$ has no point $>5$; $X\in\{0,10\}$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each has no point $=5$.

answer.value: There is a sample point with $X\ge5$

optionAnalysis.reason: False: $X$ taking values 0 and 10 with probability ½ each has mean 5 but never equals 5.
True: if every value were below 5 the mean would be below 5.
Wrong because C is always true.

pitfalls: Assuming the mean must be an attainable value.
cse-1999-a-1.verification: Checked both counterexamples: (0+10)/2 = 5 and the constant 5.

cse-1999-a-2.approach: A binary relation on $A$ is any subset of $A\times A$, so count subsets of an $n^2$-element set.

steps.title: Size of A×A
steps.body: $|A\times A|=n\cdot n=n^2$.

steps.title: Count subsets
steps.body: Each of the $n^2$ ordered pairs is either in or out of the relation: $2^{n^2}$ relations.

optionAnalysis.reason: $n^2$ is the number of ordered pairs, not relations.

cse-1999-a-3.approach: Place the $n$ zeroes first; they create $n+1$ gaps, and choose $k$ distinct gaps for the ones.

steps.title: Gaps between zeroes
steps.body: Writing the $n$ zeroes creates $n+1$ slots: before the first, between consecutive zeroes ($n-1$), and after the last.

steps.title: Choose slots
steps.body: No two ones adjacent ⇔ at most one 1 per slot. Choose $k$ of the $n+1$ slots: $\binom{n+1}{k}$ strings.

steps.title: Compare options
steps.body: $\binom{n+1}{k}$ is none of $\binom{n-1}{k}$, $\binom{n}{k}$, $\binom{n}{k+1}$ in general, so the answer is (d).

optionAnalysis.reason: $\binom{n-1}{k}$ ignores the two end slots; n = 1, k = 1 gives 0 but strings 01, 10 exist.
$\binom{n}{k}$ misses one slot; n = 1, k = 1 gives 1, actual 2.
Correct: the count is $\binom{n+1}{k}$, which is not listed.

pitfalls: Forgetting the slots at the two ends.
cse-1999-a-3.verification: n = 2 zeroes, k = 2 ones: 1010, 1001, 0101 → 3 strings = C(3,2).

cse-1999-a-4.approach: The language is all strings of length exactly $n$; a DFA must count lengths $0..n$ and needs a dead state for longer strings.

steps.title: Counting states
steps.body: States $q_0,q_1,\dots,q_n$ record the length read so far ($n+1$ states); $q_n$ is accepting. Any further symbol from $q_n$ goes to a dead state $q_d$.

steps.title: All are distinct
steps.body: For $i<j\le n$, the suffix $0^{n-i}$ is accepted after $i$ symbols but not after $j$, so the $q_i$ are pairwise distinguishable; $q_d$ accepts nothing, so it differs from every $q_i$ (each $q_i$ accepts $0^{n-i}$).

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $(n+1)+1=n+2$ states in the minimal complete DFA.

optionAnalysis.reason: $n+1$ omits the dead (trap) state required in a complete DFA.

pitfalls: Dropping the trap state — GATE counts complete DFAs.
cse-1999-a-4.verification: n = 1: language {0,1} needs start, accept and dead states → 3 = n + 2.

cse-1999-a-5.approach: Recall CFL closure: union, concatenation and Kleene star yes; intersection and complement no.

steps.title: Closed operations
steps.body: Given grammars with starts $S_1,S_2$: $S\to S_1\mid S_2$ gives union; $S\to SS_1\mid\varepsilon$ gives Kleene star.

steps.title: Not closed
steps.body: $\{a^nb^nc^m\}\cap\{a^mb^nc^n\}=\{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is not context-free, so no closure under intersection; by De Morgan with union, none under complement either.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: both have direct grammar constructions.

cse-1999-a-5.verification: The counterexample a^n b^n c^n confirms intersection fails.

cse-1999-a-6.approach: Every PDA accepting by final state can be converted to one accepting by empty stack and vice versa, so the classes coincide (both are the CFLs).

steps.title: Final state → empty stack
steps.body: Add a new bottom marker; from any final state, ε-move into a state that pops everything (including the marker).

steps.title: Empty stack → final state
steps.body: Push a new bottom marker first; when it becomes exposed (original stack empty), ε-move to a new final state.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both directions preserve the language, so $L_D=L_E$ (both are exactly the CFLs for nondeterministic PDAs).

optionAnalysis.reason: Not a proper superset — the classes are equal.
Not a proper subset — the classes are equal.

pitfalls: For deterministic PDAs empty-stack acceptance is weaker (prefix-free languages), but the question refers to PDAs in general.
cse-1999-a-6.verification: Both constructions are the standard textbook ones.

cse-1999-a-7.approach: Evaluate each option with the gate definitions.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body:
- $x$ NAND $x=\overline{x\cdot x}=\overline{x}$
- $x$ NOR $x=\overline{x+x}=\overline{x}$
- $x$ NAND $1=\overline{x\cdot1}=\overline{x}$
- $x$ NOR $1=\overline{x+1}=\overline{1}=0$

steps.title: Pick the odd one
steps.body: Only $x$ NOR 1 is the constant 0, not $\overline{x}$.

$AD+\overline{A}B$ gives 0 at $m_3$ (A = B = 0, C = D = 1), which must be 1.

cse-1999-a-10.approach: Throughput is maximised by minimising seek time per request; greedily serving the nearest cylinder does that.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Nearest cylinder next (SSTF) always picks the request with the smallest seek, so the average seek per request is lowest and requests served per second highest. FCFS ignores head position, farthest-next maximises seeks, and the elevator algorithm trades some seek time for fairness.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: SSTF gives the best throughput (at the cost of possible starvation).

optionAnalysis.reason: Good and fair, but generally a little more head movement than SSTF.

cse-1999-a-10.verification: Matches the standard comparison of disk-scheduling policies.

cse-1999-a-11.approach: A user program enters the kernel through a trap — a software interrupt instruction (e.g. INT 0x80, syscall).

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: The user process loads the call number and arguments, then executes a trap instruction; the CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps through the interrupt vector to the handler.

steps.title: Why not others
steps.body: Privileged instructions cannot be executed in user mode — that is exactly why a trap is needed.

optionAnalysis.reason: Polling is a device I/O technique, not kernel entry.
A jump cannot change the privilege mode.
User code cannot execute privileged instructions.

cse-1999-a-12.approach: Definition: a stable sort keeps equal keys in their original relative order.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: If $a_i=a_j$ with $i<j$ in the input, a stable sort places $a_i$ before $a_j$ in the output.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Option (b).

answer.value: Maintains relative order of equal elements

optionAnalysis.reason: Time complexity is unrelated (heap sort is O(n log n) and unstable).
Quick sort is divide-and-conquer but unstable.

cse-1999-a-12.verification: Insertion/merge sort are stable; heap/quick sort are not — consistent.

cse-1999-a-13.approach: Two-pointer partition: every exchange fixes one misplaced positive on the left and one misplaced negative on the right, so at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ swaps are needed.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Let $i$ scan from the left for a positive and $j$ from the right for a negative; swap while $i<j$. Each swap puts two elements into their final region.

steps.title: Worst case
steps.body: With $p$ negatives, the misplaced elements are the positives among the first $p$ slots; there are at most $\min(p,n-p)\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of them, one swap each. Worst case: all positives first, then all negatives, e.g. $+,+,-,-$ needs exactly $2=n/2$ swaps.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is none of $n-1$, $n$, $n+1$ → (d).

cse-1999-a-14.approach: Straight two-way merge sort (bottom-up) merges runs of size 1 into 2 in pass 1, then runs of 2 into 4 in pass 2.

cse-1999-a-15.approach: A vertex is an articulation point if deleting it disconnects the graph; check the attachments of the pendant vertices and the junction between the two triangles.

steps.title: Pendant attachments
steps.body: Vertex 4 hangs only on 2, and 7 hangs only on 5, so removing 2 isolates 4 and removing 5 isolates 7: **2** and **5** are articulation points.

steps.title: The junction
steps.body: Triangles {1,2,3} and {3,5,6} share only vertex 3; removing **3** separates {1,2,4} from {5,6,7}.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Removing 1 (edge 2–3 remains), 6 (edge 3–5 remains), 4 or 7 keeps the graph connected. Total = 3.

steps.title: Square repeatedly
steps.body: $a\to a^2\to a^4\to\cdots\to a^{2^k}$: each step is one multiplication. With $n=2^k$, that is $k=\log_2 n$ multiplications.

steps.title: Optimality
steps.body: Each multiplication at most doubles the largest exponent available, so reaching $n$ needs at least $\log_2 n$ multiplications.

optionAnalysis.reason: √n is more than log₂ n for large n and matches no standard method.
n exceeds even the naive count.

cse-1999-a-17.approach: Power order among these parsers: LL(1) ⊂ LR(1) and SLR ⊂ LALR ⊂ canonical LR(1).

steps.title: Hierarchy
steps.body: Canonical LR(1) items carry full lookahead per state; LALR merges states with equal cores (may add reduce–reduce conflicts); SLR uses FOLLOW sets (coarser still). LL(1) grammars are a subset of LR(1).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Canonical LR is the most powerful.

cse-1999-a-17.verification: Standard result on the LR parser hierarchy.

cse-1999-a-21.approach: In an $n\times n$ array multiplier the critical path runs through about $2n$ full-adder cells, so the delay is linear.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Partial products are formed by $n^2$ AND gates in parallel (constant delay), then added by $n-1$ rows of adders.

steps.title: Critical path
steps.body: The worst carry/sum path travels down the rows and then along the final row: about $(n-1)+(n-1)$ adder delays, i.e. $O(n)$.
